title: How can a fold make a crease at a right angle to a slanting crease?
description: A slanting crease is made on a paper. The paper is folded so that the crease lands on itself, and the new crease is at a right angle to it. The four angles around the meeting point are shown equal by tracing one and laying it on the others.
teaching_notes: One idea: fold the crease onto itself, and the new crease splits the straight angle into two equal right angles, so four right angles meet at the point. Watch for students who count only two right angles.

video_script.why: The child folds a crease at a right angle to a slanting crease and justifies the four right angles by laying angles on each other.
video_script.substitution: a paper with a slanting crease, as in the book
video_script.anchor: a paper with a slanting crease and a second crease crossing it
video_script.payoff_line: There are four right angles, each a quarter of a full turn

final_answer.value: 4 right angles, each 1/4 of a full turn; the description of the folding is open-ended
final_answer.spoken: there are four right angles, each a quarter of a full turn

maths_rules: make a slanting crease, then pick a point O on it
fold the paper so that the crease lies on itself, with the fold passing through O; the new crease is perpendicular to the first
the fold puts one half of the straight angle exactly on the other half, so the two angles are equal, and each is a right angle
at O the two creases make 4 right angles, each 1/4 of a full turn
check: trace one of the four angles and lay it on each of the others; all fit exactly
the description of the folding is open-ended: the video gives one way of folding
video_script.design: One idea: fold the crease onto itself, then the new crease makes right angles. One paper with two creases stays on the board.
open_questions: The describe-the-folding half of the book question is open-ended; the video shows one way of folding and says other ways are welcome.
